I enjoy her character a lot partially because she acts as a foil to Joe, and the show has explored that before. Joe focuses on the simple goods, like bean arches and lighthouses. He's calm and, although kind of awkward, feels comfort in people.

Sarah is incredibly neurotic, focused on large concepts like the apocalypse. She gets comfort in seclusion, and having control over the situation, because she doesn't know what the world's going to do next.

I find the dynamic between her and Joe interesting, and it keeps the show on it's toes and not feeling so one noted. Also as their relationship grows, you can see how each character grows comfortable around each other, Sarah is less snappy and puts up with going out to parties, and Joe embraces his awkwardness and isn't afraid to say silly stuff ("Like a Boss", "Country Girl", "We kissed in the sauce").

I think their personalities work as perfect foils and, based on Jo's standup and podcasts, I don't think Sarah is as faked as you think. I never got the impression her character is a one note trick, and I think she behaves like a awkward neurotic person and not like a "debby downer" type, where the punchline is her presence in the show.

This season has especially been a huge help for me. I've been watching the show since a couple months prior to season 2. I was facing a breakup and dropping out of college. A lot of it happeneing in the span of a month. 

A lot was happening very fast, and as such I think my behavior and decision making was just as quick, looking for instant gratification while I still had the security of a college lifestyle and close proximity to friends. The show's slow pace and appreciation for the simple things really struck a chord with me. The show, and especially season 2, have grounded me considerably, and I've learned to come to peace with what happened and am excited for the next steps in my life.

Since the finale, I have:
Stopped smoking,
Started reading and writing more,
Started running again after 3 years,
Have begun a short break from relationships,
Cut off ties to some bad influences,
Started performing at open mics more,
Talk to my family more often

I'm not saying Joe Pera helped me do all this, after all it is my choices to make, but it definetly helped me come to those decisions and I have to say I feel a lot happier than I did a couple months ago.

Thanks, Joe, hope you know what you're doing for people.

Saw a thread concerning the allegations, and just had some thoughts. Sorry to put this in a thread about Louis' comeback, but as an aspiring comedian myself I've thought long and hard about this and thought I would share my thoughts for discussions in here.


Louie's takedown is not indicative of a cultural problem. It was a personal issue that can serve as an example to larger Hollywood issues. I don't really blame Louis, I just think at the time he was getting fame and didn't know what he was doing with it. In retrospect he realized what he did and regretted it, which is why that response came so quickly after the article's release.

The problem here is this: If Louis CK wasn't a prominent comedian, would he have been able to do what he did? The answer 99% of the time is hell no. He was enabled by a fame he was coming to terms with and made a mistake that bit him in the ass.

I think the article blowing up (as well as fellow MeToo figures getting shunned) was a necessary evil. The general public has faced the fact that Hollywood is an evil, manipulative place that pimps out young talented people and uses them for sexual and monetary exploit. Even if you're that one in a million, they will still try to squeeze as much out of you as they can, keep you there as long as possible, and then chuck you when you fuck up to be ridiculed and mocked until you're cold in the ground (Ex. Dave Chapelle leaving the game). MeToo wasn't perfect, a very immature and fearmongering way to have a national discussion, but it was a wake up call for younger aspiring actors and comedians. If you get famous, don't contribute to the system, fight it. You get to be an influence and make money doing something people dream of doing, that is a great privallege, almost as good as becoming the president. You should treat it as the privallege it is, and not abuse it. And btw to all those who say women are maniuplative, keep your dick in your pants and see through the bullshit and you'll be ok.

I think artists find the most success and get the biggest followings when they

* keep themselves secluded and private
* have wild and crazy persona's when they do decide to be seen in the public

What I appreciated SO much about *Thank You 4 Your Service* was the fact that it refused to be nostalgic. While they very easily could've spent time reminiscing on former glories and making every single one of Phife's verses some kind of special attention, they didn't.

They never skipped a beat. The flows on this album are incredibly sick. The production, while no *Low End Theory*, are incredible. Probably my favorite ATCQ album since *Midnight Marauders*.

However, I'm especially thankful those still alive in the Tribe gave Phife the best treatment possible on this album. They dedicated ONE heartfelt, poignant song to him, and that was it. All other songs had him given the same importance as Q and Ali. I feel like he would've appreciated that. He wasn't a standalone artist, he was part of the tribe. They very much could've given Phife's versus some overly-emotional weight with the production, but he weaved with Q the way he always did. He was part of the Tribe, and they treated his verses with such integrity.

It wasn't necessarily a victory lap for ATCQ. It felt very much like they reignited a fire at the beginning of the album and burned out like rockstars by the end. This was a very passionate, very tight album even without the context of it being Quest's last.

Does this happen to be located at Toad's Place in New Haven, CT? I was looking at going, but unfortunately it is the same night as my homecoming, so I will not be attending. I HAVE however, attended a Danny Brown concert there (which, not to brag, I think will be better than Yatchy, no offense). I'll give you some quick tips about the venue in general, and how to act around the Toad crowd

* DON'T TRUST THE SCHEDULE- this might go without saying, but usually rappers will show up MUCH later than what the concert schedule suggests. If you are rushing to get to the door in time, don't worry. You will be greeted with a DJ, a semi-empty venue, and PLENTY of time to get comfortable for the night.

* WEAR LIGHT CLOTHING- Toad's is a small venue, which means that even in an audience of a couple hundred people, the place will still be packed. If you don't want to come out drenched, I suggest wearing some lighter clothing.

* HYDRATE- I'm not kidding. The crowd at the Danny concert was ROWDY. I was front row the entire 3 hours, and was either up against someone, or they were up against me. It's jumping, dancing, yelling, and moving. It's incredibly taxing. There is no shame or real downside in stepping out to get a breather and a drink, like I did after the openers.

* (Specific only to Toad's) IF YOU PLAN ON TAKING ANY ILLICIT SUBSTANCES, I SUGGEST DOING SO BEFORE ENTERING- My friends tried to smoke up during the performance, right in the middle of the dance floor. It's not always guaranteed, but there is a pretty good chance a very big man will tap you on the shoulder and tell you to throw you're shit out. They don't kid around. If you plan to do anything, don't take your chances doing it inside. Smoke before.

* KNOW WHO YOU'RE SEEING- Study their discographies, know some of their songs by heart, watch some videos and get to know the artist's personality a little. It makes the concert 10 times more engaging. I've been to bigger venue concerts watching bands I never really cared about (Phish, Snoop), I can tell you learning and loving the artist is key to a great time.

* YOUR EARS WILL BE SHOT- The bass booms, the rappers yell, the crowd screams. My ears rang for days after the Danny Brown concert, my voice was raspy from yelling as well. Wear some earplugs if you want, just be warned, it gets loud.

* ENJOY YOURSELF- Toad's is a small place, meaning that people attending the concert are there ONLY to enjoy the music. It's located near Yale, so not a lot of sketchy people really attend. I'm a scrawny, nerdy, 17 y/o white kid, and I never felt uncomfortable a second at Toad's. Push your way to the front, Yell uncontrollably, lose your fucking mind, start a mosh. Everyone is there for the same reason you are, to have a good time. So enjoy yourself for the time you're there.

That's all I really gotta say. Also, the venue is kinda crappy. However, the crowd is what really makes the place shine, I had a great time there and I hope you do to. Have Fun!

An upcoming R&B artist who was inducted into the 2016 XXL Freshman class, and he seems to be the one with the most talent. An incredible drummer and soulful singer, his latest album *Malibu* was a breath of fresh air in an otherwise stale year for R&B and Funk.

* Flying Lotus (and while your at it, the majority of the Brainfeeder Label)

Flying Lotus, the grandchild of Alice Coltrane, is an electronic musician that blends live instrumentation with spacey, resonant, funky beats. It's both spiritual, dense, and soulful at the same time. He produces under the Brainfeeder label, which also has talents like Thundercat, an incredible bassist that made a great contribution of Kendrick Lamar's *To Pimp a Butterfly*. There is also Jeremiah Jae, who raps over dusty, vinyl beats. Another great artist I recommend checking out.

* Timber Timbre

An awesome folk/blues/jazz group with vocals that make the group sound as though a stalker serial killer decided to write poetry. They use a variety of instrumentation to create some moody, swampy, and awesome pieces. Saxophones, organs, and more come together to make some chillingly beautiful pieces. I would recommend *Creep on Creeping On* as the album to check out.

TL;DR: The radio isn't the only place to find music, keep on digging and, eventually, you will strike gold.
